newsitem.title: INDIA: India can have higher current deficit-Chidambaram.
newsitem.headline: India can have higher current deficit-Chidambaram.

text.p: India can afford a rise in its current account deficit in the external sector to boost investment in the economy, former finance minister P.Chidambaram said on Tuesday.

Chidambaram, who ended 10 months as finance minister on Monday after his regional party pulled out of the ruling coalition, told a business conference that a higher current account deficit could help economic growth.
India needed a savings rate of around 30 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and investment of around 32 percent to attain an intended annual growth rate of 8.0 percent, he said.
The gap between savings and investment could be met with a higher current account deficit resulting from an inflow of foreign investment, Chidambaram said.
"There is no danger if the current account deficit rises to 2.0 percent or even 2.4 percent," he said.

Chidambaram, a key architect of India's six-year-old economic reform programme, said he differed with the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), which said in a background paper prepared for the conference that India's current account deficit was high.

The current account deficit for 1996/97 (April-March) is currently estimated at 1.4 percent of the GDP, as against 1.7 percent in 1995/96. It represents the gap between imports and exports of merchandise as well as services.
India's gross domestic savings rate averaged 23.9 of the GDP between 1992 and 1996, and gross domestic investment 25.3, indicating an average current account deficit of 1.4 percent.

Chidambaram said India needed to boost both savings and investment to sustain a growth rate of 8.0 percent. India's GDP is estimated to have grown 6.8 percent in 1996/97, compared with 7.1 percent in 1995/96.
India must boldly free up imports, allow more foreign borrowings by Indian firms and invest in education, healthcare and environment to sustain high growth, he said.
